utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-94-2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it please the Court, Dirk Ryneveld and Dermot Groome for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Howard Morrison for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can you hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? Can you hear the proceedings in a language which you understand, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a Status Conference held in accordance with the Rules and within the time limited by those Rules. Mr. Ryneveld, is there any matter which you wish to raise at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Not that occurs to me at the moment. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, there are just three points. The first relates to an incident or two incidents which occurred in September of last year. I've informed my learned friends for the Prosecution about these matters, and I raise them purely for information purposes only. I don't seek any order or determination by the Court today. The relatives of the accused still live in Vlasenica in Bosnia and in the Republika Srpska, and one of the witnesses whose statement has been served upon the Defence names people other than the accused. One of those persons named by that witness has taken exception to the fact that his name has been mentioned, and his son and wife have, on two occasions, issued fairly dramatic threats to the sister of the accused in Vlasenica. I take some comfort from the fact that the last of these threats was issued on the 26th of September of last year. They've only just been recently brought to my notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Tell me, does the witness who made this statement identify your client as the source of the reference to these other people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's the bizarre circumstances of this case. There is no such allegation or reference by the witness. No, it's simply an assumption that has been made, apparently, that for some reason the accused is culpable as to that. I simply raise this matter at this stage, and I've indicated it to the Prosecution. If anything further arises and there is a necessity to ask for any form of protective measures, the Court is forewarned of the nature of the incident

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose there is very little you can do about the ignorant assumptions of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. That's the first incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: The second matter is this: Of course Your Honour and Your Honour's colleague will have seen the documentation which has been filed in this case. Although there is no specific determination in the decision that emanated from the Tribunal on the 20th of March of this year, am I correct in making the assumption that it's effectively a determination that the Prosecution has complied with Rule 66 as of the 20th of March?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure what document you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's the determination, decision on the third motion by the Prosecution for protective measures dated the 20th of March and signed by Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I remember that document, but all we can do is to say these are the protective measures which will be applicable. If the Prosecution has served all of the statements that it is required to under Rule 66 which comply with those protective measures, then the Prosecution has complied with it. But that depends upon what you say, not what we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for that and that's precisely why I raise the query. As far as the Defence are concerned, I accept the bona fides that I have been told by the Prosecution that they have complied insofar as they are physically able to do so at this stage with all the requirements and on the assumption therefore that Mr. Ryneveld makes an deemed that the Prosecution has complied with Rule 66, I can take no objection to that for the purposes of time running for purposes of Rule 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, unless we had evidence upon which we could make a determination, it could only be by agreement. I don't like deeming anything, but if we note an agreement that the Prosecution has complied with 66(A)(i), then you are in a situation in that time starts to run.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, so be it. We are in agreement. I do accept that as of today, and I have been orally informed this morning that that is the position, that the Prosecution have done all that they can do, so if time starts to run as from today, that's 30 days as from today in the normal circumstances, which leads me to the third issue that I want to raise. This is purely a matter of incidence or, rather, coincidence. I've recently found out that I have to go into hospital on the 4th of April to Leicester Royal Infirmary in England for surgery. It's invasive surgery. I'm told that I'm likely to be out of action, for all effective purposes, for something in the order of 14 days, assuming there are no complications, which is an assumption I'm happy to make. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thirty days, I think, is the 28th of April. You're asking for an extra two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm just asking for an extra two weeks from that date so that the period that I shall be ineffective or even more ineffective is taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the Prosecution consents to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We certainly do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't have a diary now, but we'll make it so that it doesn't fall on an awkward day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, if I could have until the -- Friday the 11th of May would be, I think, a suitable day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was going to suggest the following Friday just so that you've got plenty of time up your sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, out of an abundance of caution, I gratefully accept that, if it could be the 18th of May. Of course I'm not going to use all that time if it's not necessary. I will serve any motions as soon as they are ready to be served, but if that time under Rule 72 could be extended till 18th of May, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison, about this proposed application which you forewarned us of previously challenging the jurisdiction on the basis of the nature of the arrest, the Appeals Chamber has accepted that the onus is on you to establish your case. If you seek the assistance of anybody else to provide you with the material, you do have to show that there is a likelihood, I suppose, a likelihood or it's on the cards, as one Judge put it, that that person you seek assistance from can give you that assistance. Now, it's not to be a fishing expedition. I don't want this point to arise later. That's why I'm raising it now. You will have to put on something to demonstrate that there is an issue which we have to determine before you will get an order from us that anybody else gives you assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, the reality of the position is that the only two sources of information which would otherwise remain confidential or subject to an aura of secrecy would be either the Office of the Prosecutor or SFOR themselves. They're the only two sources of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But in order to get any assistance from either the OTP or SFOR, you would have to demonstrate to us that there is something that -- some likelihood that they will be able to give you that assistance. Mr. Todorovic, if you remember, thought that he had done that, although there was some confusion there about the onus of proof, by simply tendering a third-hand, hearsay item off the Internet, and he failed, and the Appeals Chamber agreed with the Trial Chamber that he had failed. He then came along and he gave evidence, and it was the evidence which he gave which persuaded the Trial Chamber that SFOR would be able to assist, because he gave evidence of the circumstances in which he arrived at the air base which was controlled by SFOR. You don't have to prove that SFOR was in some way improper at this stage. You have to only demonstrate that their records may well assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, of course an evidentiary hearing where the accused himself gives evidence upon oath is a possibility. He's the best possible source of the information of what happened to him in any particular period of time. There can't be a better source than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And there would be a limitation upon the extent to which the Prosecution could cross-examine him, rather like a voir dire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. But -- and I will certainly make an application for such an evidentiary hearing if the Prosecution indicate to me that they contest that he was, in fact, in some way, and I use the word as a matter of generality at the moment, kidnapped from Serbia and removed, against his will, into Bosnia-Herzegovina and there handed over to members of SFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That leads me to the next issue that I want to raise with you. Bearing in mind the turmoil that the SFOR order has produced, and I'm not worried about the political ramifications about it despite what Mr. Ryneveld's colleague tried to put before us in that hearing, but I'm talking about the legal ramifications with appeals and every country from NATO putting on an appearance, and they're even now trying to persuade the Appeals Chamber to hear the appeal notwithstanding the removal of the order. There is another very real issue that we have to determine, and it will be for the first time, I think, by an International Tribunal, and that is whether misconduct, if I could use that in a very general sense, on the part of somebody other than the Prosecutor is relevant. As you would be aware, most national systems take the view that this is not a game of cricket, and if people try to avoid being arrested and they are arrested in circumstances which may not comply with everybody's human rights, nevertheless, provided the Prosecution or the Tribunal are not involved in it, it doesn't matter. Now, I put that in a very general sense. That is, as I say, a fresh issue which has never been determined. The Prosecution, in the Todorovic case, was very keen for the Trial Chamber to determine that first, and for various reasons, the Trial Chamber decide against doing so, because there was at least an issue which they felt had to be determined. But rather than put everybody through the turmoil of another SFOR order and appeal and the delays that will occur, it may be preferable for that other issue to be determined first. If, and I'm not saying anybody's got a particular view, but if that was determined against you, that would be a matter which could be dealt with by the Appeals Chamber reasonably speedily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, with great respect, I think that's eminently sensible, if I may say so, because the last thing that Mr. Nikolic wants to do is go through the -- as it were, the delays and the turmoil of Todorovic, and it's the last thing I want to do, and I'm sure it's the last thing that the OTP want to do. If there is a question of a point of law to be determined, as Your Honour indicates, then I would be more than content to draft that point of law for determination, to annex to that motion for a determination the authorities that I rely upon and indeed authorities that I can find that may assist the Tribunal in general, and to have that point taken as a preliminary point of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There has been some publications on this issue. In the Judge McDonald book, there is an article which refers briefly to some of those cases, the article by Susan Lamb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've read that, and I'm going to shamelessly exploit it and adopt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: She's written one also in the international law journal or one of them, one of the British ones, in more detail, I think, but that seems to me that if you want to pursue this preliminary motion, we could start on that. The concern I have is that your client may have to languish in custody longer than he should otherwise awaiting his trial. The ad litem judges, of course, will certainly pick up the speed of the list, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Without having taken instructions, and Mr. Nikolic hears what I say, looking at the court diary and calendar, I would have thought it unlikely that such a preliminary point was going to extend by any significant period the question of a trial date in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't assume that too much. This case will not necessarily be tried by Trial Chamber II, and Trial Chamber I, whatever its composition may be, will be free to start hearing cases very shortly, and the other two cases which are ahead of you on our list are likely to start as soon as the ad litem judges are appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, this is a matter of great significance to the accused, and it may be a matter of great significance to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not here to try and make law, just as your client is not here to make sure his name is on a leading case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: No, but I look ahead and see a position whereby one, for the sake of getting an earlier trial date, takes shortcuts, only to find out that there is another case, similar case, in future where a determination is made which would have had impact upon the client's case, and then one is left asking that "what-if" question, which is a question I don't want to ask. I mean the resolution of the speed of this matter is really in part a factor of how quickly, first of all, I deal with it and how quickly the Prosecution responds. I think we can work together on this and within the time scale that has already been allocated for the response to Rule 72, then I am sure that a motion can be put together with all the authorities and perhaps even heard within that time scale or at least listed within that time scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right then. I'll leave that for your consideration and your discussion with the Prosecution. Mr. Ryneveld, do you want to say anything about this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No. To echo my friend's remarks, it seems a reasonable solution to the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may not be a solution but it may be. It just struck me as being perhaps a quicker way to get on with the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I whole-heartedly endorse Your Honour's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One thing though, Mr. Ryneveld, if I may raise with you, I imagine that the 80 counts that the draftsmen of this indictment produced earned the draftsmen, whoever that may have been, some sort of an award up in the OTP, but we now have some authority about cumulative convictions. Nobody can actually stop the Prosecution being silly and multiplying unnecessarily the counts in the indictment unless it produces an injustice, but I do suggest that somebody might like to look to see just how necessary 80 counts really are in this case. See, in the current detention centre case we're dealing with now, the Prosecution very wisely withdrew all the grave breaches because it required them to prove something which was not easy and unnecessary, and the relationship between Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute have now become fairly clear from the Kunarac case, and the internal duplication within Article 5 is a matter which will clearly arise in our current case. So it may be that the Prosecution, instead of making awards for the largest number of counts, can look at it sensibly as to how the trial is going to be conducted, and it may like to slightly reduce them at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I can assure Your Honour that my co-counsel and I have already looked at that possibility, and although I can't make any undertakings at this point because I need to discuss this with the powers that be, that is something we are certainly looking at. We're not anxious to proceed with 80 counts either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you can tell the draftsmen that. Very well, then. Is there anything else that you want to raise, either of you, under the Rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're very grateful for your attendance, and we will make a formal order deeming time to have commenced to run, and we grant an extension of time for any preliminary motion under Rule 72 until the 18th of May, and, Mr. Morrison, we hope you are successful. We're adjourned.
